act_vs_pred.title: Actual vs. Predicted
act_vs_pred.description: A scatter plot comparing ground truth values against model predictions. A dashed 45-degree line is used to represent a perfect prediction.
act_vs_pred.insights: Points hugging the diagonal line mean high accuracy. If points drift away from the line at higher values, the model struggles with larger numbers.
act_vs_pred.example: If a house sold for $500k and the model predicted $480k, this plot visualizes that $20k gap. Perfect predictions sit exactly on the line.

res_dist.title: Residuals Distribution
res_dist.description: A histogram showing the distribution of the model's errors (Actual - Predicted) to see if they follow a normal, bell-shaped curve.
res_dist.insights: A balanced, centered curve means errors are random. A skewed curve means the model is systematically overpredicting or underpredicting.
res_dist.example: If the bell curve leans heavily to the left, the model systematically predicts house prices higher than they actually are.

res_vs_pred.title: Residuals vs. Predicted
res_vs_pred.description: Plots the errors against the predicted values to check if the error magnitude changes as predictions get larger.
res_vs_pred.insights: A random scatter around the zero-line is ideal. A funnel shape (fan-out) means the model loses accuracy on larger predictions (heteroscedasticity).
res_vs_pred.example: Reveals if the model's margin of error is $10k for cheap apartments, but blows up to $200k for luxury mansions.

res_vs_act.title: Residuals vs. Actual
res_vs_act.description: Plots the errors directly against the true target values to see how the model behaves across the actual domain of the data.
res_vs_act.insights: Helps spot specific ranges in the real-world data where the model completely falls apart.
res_vs_act.example: Shows if the model is highly accurate for middle-class homes but consistently fails for ultra-rare, high-end estates.

qq.title: Normal Q-Q Plot
qq.description: A diagnostic plot that compares the distribution of the model's errors to a theoretical normal distribution.
qq.insights: Points tracking the straight reference line mean errors are normally distributed. Tails drifting away indicate extreme, unexpected outlier errors.
qq.example: If the dots curve sharply at the top right, the model is making rare, massive miscalculations on a few specific houses.

scale_loc.title: Scale-Location Plot
scale_loc.description: Plots the square root of absolute errors against predictions. It makes it easier to spot if error variance is spreading out.
scale_loc.insights: A flat, horizontal trend line means the prediction uncertainty is equal across the board (homoscedasticity).
scale_loc.example: A flat line confirms you can trust the model's confidence just as much for a $100k house as for a $1M house.

post_pred.title: Posterior Predictive Density
post_pred.description: Overlays the distribution shape of the actual target values with the distribution shape of the model's predictions.
post_pred.insights: Shows if the model is capturing the real-world demographics of the data, including multiple peaks (bimodal data).
post_pred.example: If the real housing market has a peak for suburban homes and a peak for city condos, this shows if the model captured both peaks or just averaged them out.

leverage.title: Residuals vs. Leverage
leverage.description: Identifies extreme data points that have a disproportionate, pulling effect on the model's overall logic.
leverage.insights: High leverage points in the top/bottom right corners (beyond Cook's distance) are outliers skewing the entire model.
leverage.example: Flags a single $50M castle in a dataset of normal homes that is artificially pulling the model's pricing logic upward.

outliers.title: Outlier Feature Analysis
outliers.description: Plots the standardized residuals against the specific feature that has the strongest relationship with the model's largest errors.
outliers.insights: Highlights the exact variable whose extreme values or specific ranges are causing the model to generate massive errors, exposing critical blind spots.
outliers.example: Reveals that the houses the model priced worst were consistently those built before 1950, showing that 'Year Built' is the root cause of these extreme errors.

metrics.title: Performance Metrics Summary
metrics.description: A consolidated table of the model's vital signs (R², RMSE, Accuracy, F1-Score) across training and testing data.
metrics.insights: The ultimate quick-glance check for model health and overfitting. Training and testing scores should be relatively close.
metrics.example: An R² of 0.95 on training data but 0.60 on test data immediately flags that the model memorized the data rather than learning it.

cm.title: Confusion Matrix
cm.description: A grid showing exactly where a classification model guessed right (True Positives/Negatives) and where it got confused.
cm.insights: Breaks down total accuracy into specific mistakes: false alarms vs. missed detections.
cm.example: Shows out of 100 actual frauds, the model caught 85 (True Positives) but let 15 slip through (False Negatives).

class_dist.title: Class Distribution
class_dist.description: A bar chart comparing the real-world proportion of classes against what the model is predicting.
class_dist.insights: Checks if the model is taking the lazy route by just guessing the majority class all the time.
class_dist.example: If frauds are only 1% of the real data, but the model is predicting 10% of transactions as fraud, it is far too aggressive.

prob_dist.title: Probability Confidence Distribution
prob_dist.description: Shows how confident the model was when making predictions, separated by the true class of the data.
prob_dist.insights: A good model pushes predictions to the extremes (0% or 100%). A confused model has a lump of predictions around 50%.
prob_dist.example: Ideally, valid transactions are clustered at 5% fraud probability, and actual frauds are clustered near 95%, with very few in the middle.

roc.title: Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC)
roc.description: Plots the trade-off between catching true positives and triggering false alarms across different strictness thresholds.
roc.insights: The higher the curve hugs the top left corner (high AUC), the better the model is at separating the classes.
roc.example: An AUC of 0.95 means the model is excellent at ranking a fraudulent transaction higher on the suspicion list than a valid one.

pr.title: Precision-Recall Curve
pr.description: Evaluates the trade-off between catching all positive cases (Recall) and ensuring every positive guess is correct (Precision).
pr.insights: The gold standard for highly imbalanced data (where one class is rare). High curves indicate robust performance.
pr.example: If catching every fraud means freezing thousands of innocent accounts (low precision), this curve helps find the sweet spot to balance the business impact.

misclass.title: Misclassification Feature Analysis
misclass.description: Analyzes the data points the model got wrong to find common traits among the errors.
misclass.insights: Identifies the specific profiles or customer segments where the classification logic breaks down.
misclass.example: Reveals that valid transactions wrongly blocked as fraud usually happen when customers are traveling abroad.

calibration.title: Calibration Curve (Reliability)
calibration.description: Checks if the predicted probabilities match the actual real-world frequencies. If the model says 80% chance of rain, it should actually rain 8 out of 10 times.
calibration.insights: A curve hugging the diagonal means the model's confidence scores are trustworthy. Deviations mean it is overconfident or underconfident.
calibration.example: Shows that when the model predicts a 90% chance of fraud, in reality, only 50% of those transactions are fraudulent (overconfidence).

threshold.title: Decision Threshold Analysis
threshold.description: Displays how Precision, Recall, and F1-Score change as you adjust the cut-off probability (threshold) for making a positive prediction.
threshold.insights: Helps you manually find the perfect cut-off point to balance false alarms and missed detections according to your business needs.
threshold.example: Instead of the default 50% cut-off, this chart shows that dropping the threshold to 30% catches double the frauds with only a tiny drop in precision.

shap_summary.title: Global Feature Importance (SHAP)
shap_summary.description: Shows the average impact of each feature on the model's predictions across the entire dataset.
shap_summary.insights: Features at the top are the primary drivers of the model's logic. This reveals what the model actually cares about.
shap_summary.example: If 'Age' has the highest bar, it means Age causes the largest swings in the model's final decision compared to any other factor.

shap_beeswarm.title: SHAP Beeswarm Plot
shap_beeswarm.description: A beeswarm/strip plot where each dot is one sample. The x-position shows the SHAP value (impact direction), and the color shows the feature value (red=high, blue=low).
shap_beeswarm.insights: Combines importance AND direction in one view. A wide horizontal spread means high variance in that feature's impact. Color gradients reveal if high feature values push predictions up or down.
shap_beeswarm.example: If 'Age' dots fan right and are red, older patients strongly push the prediction toward positive. Blue dots on the left mean young patients lower the risk prediction.

shap_waterfall.title: Local Explanation (Waterfall)
shap_waterfall.description: Breaks down exactly how the model arrived at its prediction for a specific, individual data point selected in the table.
shap_waterfall.insights: Starting from the average baseline, each bar shows how a specific feature value pushed the prediction up (red) or down (blue).
shap_waterfall.example: Shows that while the baseline price was $300k, the house being built in 1990 added $50k, but having only 1 bathroom subtracted $30k, resulting in a $320k prediction.
